## Introduction

[Lab 1](class6_lab1.html){target="_blank"} showed the SVM ideas on simulated
data: hyperplanes, support vectors, the cost dial, kernels. This lab puts them
to work on real tumor biopsies, in two parts:

1. **The tumor example from the slides.** Real biopsy data, the same two
   features (cell size and cell shape uniformity), then all nine, across three
   kernels.
2. **Variable selection for classification.** Thirty correlated tumor features:
   ordinary logistic regression breaks, and the lasso picks a handful.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install
needed. Packages and data load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds
on first load. Cells run when you click **Run Code**. Run them in order from
the top of each part, because later cells use objects made by earlier ones.

**Remember the warning from Lab 1:** the software cost `C` runs *opposite* to
the slides' budget $C$. Large software `C` = violations are expensive = narrow
margin.

We fit every SVM with `caret::train()`, following
[Lab 5](../../05-classification-1/code/class5_lab1.html): `method =
"svmLinear"`, `"svmPoly"`, and `"svmRadial"` all call `kernlab` underneath.

# Part 1 — The tumor example from the slides

The slides motivated SVMs with benign vs. malignant tumors plotted on **cell
size uniformity** and **cell shape uniformity**. Those come from the Wisconsin
breast-cancer biopsy data, which ships with the `MASS` package as `biopsy`:
699 biopsies, nine cytology scores each rated 1–10, and the diagnosis.

```{webr}
library(MASS)
library(dplyr)

tumor <- biopsy |>
  na.omit() |>                      # 16 biopsies are missing bare_nuclei
  transmute(clump_thickness = V1, cell_size = V2, cell_shape = V3,
            adhesion = V4, epithelial_size = V5, bare_nuclei = V6,
            chromatin = V7, nucleoli = V8, mitoses = V9,
            class = factor(class, levels = c("benign", "malignant"),
                           labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

dim(tumor)
table(tumor$class)
```

683 complete biopsies, 65% benign. The scores are whole numbers from 1 to 10,
so many patients share exactly the same (size, shape) pair — we **jitter** the
points slightly so they don't stack on top of each other:

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(tumor, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, colour = class)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0.25, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(x = "Cell Size Uniformity", y = "Cell Shape Uniformity",
       colour = "Tumor Class",
       title = "Tumor classification based on biomarkers") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Mostly separable, with a band of overlap in the middle — a job for the soft
margin.

### Split, then tune the cost by cross-validation

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
library(caret)

set.seed(2155)
idx <- createDataPartition(tumor$class, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train_data <- tumor[idx, ]
test_data  <- tumor[-idx, ]

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(2155)
svm_2 <- train(class ~ cell_size + cell_shape, data = train_data,
               method = "svmLinear", trControl = ctrl,
               preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
               tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))

ggplot(svm_2$results, aes(C, Accuracy)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "cost C (log scale)", y = "10-fold CV accuracy",
       title = "Cross-validated accuracy across the cost grid") +
  theme_bw()
svm_2$bestTune
```

Cross-validation picks `C = 8`, but look at the y-axis: accuracy only runs
from 0.934 to 0.951 across a 1,000-fold range of `C`. On this data the cost
barely matters. That is common — and it's why we tune on a log-spaced grid
rather than agonizing over one value.

### The fitted boundary

`predict()` on a grid of (size, shape) values paints the regions the SVM
assigns to each class. `caret` applies the same centering and scaling to the
grid that it applied to the training data.

```{webr}
grid <- expand.grid(cell_size  = seq(0.5, 10.5, length.out = 120),
                    cell_shape = seq(0.5, 10.5, length.out = 120))
grid$pred <- predict(svm_2, grid)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, fill = pred), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(data = train_data, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, colour = class),
              width = 0.25, height = 0.25, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() + ggsci::scale_fill_aaas(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cell Size Uniformity", y = "Cell Shape Uniformity",
       colour = "Tumor Class", title = "Linear SVM on two biomarkers") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### How well does it do on the test set?

As in Lab 5 we set `positive = "Malignant"`, so **sensitivity** is the share of
cancers we catch.

```{webr}
confusionMatrix(predict(svm_2, test_data), test_data$class,
                positive = "Malignant")
```

With just two features the linear SVM gets **95.3%** of the 170 test biopsies
right, catching 56 of 59 cancers (sensitivity 0.949) while clearing 106 of 111
benign tumors (specificity 0.955).

### All nine features, three kernels

Now use every score, and compare the three kernels from class. All three go
through the same `train()` call; only `method` changes. **This is the heaviest
cell in Part 1** (the polynomial grid fits 270 models) — give it a moment.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
f_all <- class ~ .

set.seed(2155)
svm_lin <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))
set.seed(2155)
svm_poly <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmPoly",
                  trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                  tuneLength = 3)
set.seed(2155)
svm_rad <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmRadial",
                 trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                 tuneLength = 6)

summarise_svm <- function(model, name) {
  cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(model, test_data), test_data$class,
                        positive = "Malignant")
  data.frame(Model = name,
             Accuracy    = round(cm$overall[["Accuracy"]], 3),
             Sensitivity = round(cm$byClass[["Sensitivity"]], 3),
             Specificity = round(cm$byClass[["Specificity"]], 3))
}

rbind(summarise_svm(svm_2,    "Linear, 2 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_lin,  "Linear, 9 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_poly, "Polynomial, 9 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_rad,  "Radial, 9 features"))
```

- **More features help:** going from two scores to nine lifts accuracy from
  0.953 to 0.971 and sensitivity from 0.949 to 0.983 (one missed cancer instead
  of three).
- **More flexible kernels don't:** linear, polynomial, and radial land within
  one test biopsy of each other. Cross-validation even picked the *smallest*
  cost on the grid for the linear kernel — the widest, most forgiving margin.
- The lesson from the ring in Lab 1, in reverse: a kernel only pays off when the true boundary
  is curved. These cytology scores rise together as a tumor turns malignant,
  so a straight cut is already about as good as it gets. Try the linear kernel
  first; reach for a kernel only when CV says it helps.

# Part 2 — Variable selection for classification

Everything so far used a few hand-picked features. Real problems often come
with many correlated candidates, and we would like the data to tell us which
ones matter. Back to the **Wisconsin Diagnostic (WDBC)** data from Lab 5, this
time with **all 30 features**: ten nuclear measurements, each recorded as a
mean, a standard error, and a "worst" value.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(caret)

wdbc <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                            labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

set.seed(2155)
idx <- createDataPartition(wdbc$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
wtrain <- wdbc[idx, ]
wtest  <- wdbc[-idx, ]

c(train = nrow(wtrain), test = nrow(wtest), features = ncol(wdbc) - 1)
```

### Why not just throw everything into logistic regression?

```{webr}
full_glm <- glm(diagnosis ~ ., data = wtrain, family = binomial)
summary(abs(coef(full_glm)))
```

R warns that the algorithm **did not converge** and that fitted probabilities
are **numerically 0 or 1**. The training tumors are perfectly separable in 30
dimensions, so the likelihood keeps improving as the coefficients grow —
the median coefficient is about 500 and the largest about 44,000, on the
log-odds scale. These estimates mean nothing, and
(spoiler) the model does worst of everything we'll try on the test set.

### The lasso: logistic regression with a penalty

The fix is the same one we used for regression in [Lab 3](../../03-regression-1/code/class3_lab1.html): add a penalty. The
**lasso** maximizes

$$\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \log L(\beta;\, y_i, x_i)}_{\text{logistic log-likelihood}} \; - \; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| .$$

The absolute-value penalty does two jobs at once: it keeps the coefficients
finite, and it sets many of them **exactly to zero** — so fitting the model
*is* selecting variables. $\lambda$ controls how many survive. `glmnet` fits
the whole path of $\lambda$ values in one call (`alpha = 1` is the lasso;
`alpha = 0` would be ridge).

The features are on very different scales (areas in the hundreds,
smoothness around 0.1), and the penalty treats every $\beta_j$ alike, so we
**standardize first**, using the training means and SDs for both sets.

```{webr}
library(glmnet)

X_train <- scale(as.matrix(wtrain[, -1]))
X_test  <- scale(as.matrix(wtest[, -1]),
                 center = attr(X_train, "scaled:center"),
                 scale  = attr(X_train, "scaled:scale"))

lasso_path <- glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
plot(lasso_path, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
```

Read the plot right to left: at large $\lambda$ (right) every coefficient is
zero; as $\lambda$ shrinks, features enter one at a time. The numbers along
the top count how many are in the model.

### Pick your own λ

Choose a $\lambda$ and see which features survive and how the test accuracy
responds. Change `log10_lambda`, then click **Run Code** again. This cell
reuses `lasso_path`, `X_test`, and `wtest` from the cells above.

```{webr}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
log10_lambda <- -1          # try -3.5, -2, -1, -0.5

lam <- 10^log10_lambda
b   <- as.matrix(coef(lasso_path, s = lam))[-1, 1]
b   <- b[b != 0]
acc <- mean(predict(lasso_path, X_test, s = lam, type = "class") == wtest$diagnosis)

if (length(b) == 0) {
  b <- c("(no features selected)" = 0)
}
coefs <- data.frame(feature = names(b), beta = unname(b))
coefs$effect <- factor(ifelse(coefs$beta > 0, "raises P(Malignant)",
                              "lowers P(Malignant)"),
                       levels = c("lowers P(Malignant)", "raises P(Malignant)"))

ggplot(coefs, aes(beta, reorder(feature, abs(beta)), fill = effect)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("lowers P(Malignant)" = "#3B4992",
                               "raises P(Malignant)" = "#EE0000"),
                    name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "standardized coefficient", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("λ = %.4f   |   %d of 30 features kept   |   test accuracy %.1f%%",
                       lam, sum(coefs$beta != 0), 100 * acc)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A few settings to try:

| log₁₀(λ) | features kept | test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| −3.5 | 21 | 97.9% |
| −2.0 | 8 | 97.9% |
| −1.0 | 4 | 95.1% |
| −0.5 | 2 | 69.7% |

From 21 features down to 8 the test accuracy **does not move**: those extra
13 features were redundant. Around 6 features it starts to slip, and at
2 the model has thrown away real signal. Somewhere in between is the smallest
model that is still as good as the big one — which is what cross-validation
will find.

### Letting cross-validation choose λ

`cv.glmnet()` runs 10-fold CV along the whole path. It reports two choices:
`lambda.min` (the lowest CV error) and `lambda.1se` (the largest $\lambda$
within one standard error of that minimum — the simplest model that is
statistically as good). For selection we usually prefer `lambda.1se`.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
set.seed(2155)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                      alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
plot(lasso_cv)

b_1se <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
selected <- rownames(b_1se)[b_1se[, 1] != 0][-1]   # drop the intercept
selected
```

The `lambda.1se` model keeps **10 of the 30 features**. Notice what's
there: mostly **"worst"** measurements (the most abnormal cells in the image)
and the **concavity / concave points** family — the irregular, indented cell
outlines a pathologist looks for. Of radius, perimeter, and area — three
near-copies of "how big is the nucleus" — the lasso keeps area_worst and
radius_worst but not perimeter: with correlated features, the lasso tends to
keep one or two representatives and drop the rest.

### Does selecting features cost us anything?

Compare, on the same 142 test tumors: the unpenalized logistic model, the
lasso, ridge (penalized but no selection), and a linear SVM trained on all 30
features vs. only the lasso's picks.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
set.seed(2155)
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                      alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)

set.seed(2155)
svm_all <- train(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))
set.seed(2155)
svm_sel <- train(X_train[, selected], wtrain$diagnosis, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))

glm_pred <- ifelse(predict(full_glm, wtest, type = "response") > 0.5,
                   "Malignant", "Benign")
acc <- function(pred) round(mean(pred == wtest$diagnosis), 3)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Logistic, no penalty", "Lasso logistic (lambda.1se)",
            "Ridge logistic (lambda.1se)", "Linear SVM, all features",
            "Linear SVM, lasso-selected features"),
  Features = c(30, length(selected), 30, 30, length(selected)),
  Test_accuracy = c(acc(glm_pred),
                    acc(predict(lasso_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "class")),
                    acc(predict(ridge_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "class")),
                    acc(predict(svm_all, X_test)),
                    acc(predict(svm_sel, X_test[, selected])))
)
```

- **The unpenalized model is worst (0.944)** — the inflated coefficients from
  above do real damage on new data.
- **Lasso with 10 features = ridge with 30 = SVM with 30 (all 0.979).** We got
  a model a third the size at no cost in accuracy, and one that names which
  measurements matter.
- **The SVM on the lasso's 10 features is one tumor behind (0.972).** Variable
  selection by one method can be handed to another.
- Everything — the standardization, the λ choice, the selected list — came from
  the **training** tumors only. Selecting features on all the data and then
  "testing" on part of it leaks information and makes the test accuracy look
  better than it is.

### How stable is the selection?

The lasso's choice depends on the data it saw — including the random
assignment of CV folds. Re-run the CV with 10 different fold assignments and
count how often each feature is picked. To keep it quick we search a 30-point
λ grid around where `lambda.1se` landed. **This is the slowest cell in the
lab** — allow up to a minute.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-1, -3, length.out = 30)

picks <- sapply(1:10, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  cvfit <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                     alpha = 1, nfolds = 10, lambda = lambda_grid)
  as.matrix(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1, 1] != 0
})

freq <- sort(rowMeans(picks), decreasing = TRUE)
freq <- freq[freq > 0]

ggplot(data.frame(feature = names(freq), freq = freq),
       aes(freq, reorder(feature, freq))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3B4992") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "share of 10 CV runs that selected the feature", y = NULL,
       title = "Lasso selection frequency across CV fold assignments") +
  theme_bw()
```

Seven features are chosen in **every** run — concavity_mean,
concave_points_mean, radius_worst, texture_worst, smoothness_worst,
concave_points_worst, symmetry_worst. Those you can trust. The rest come and
go with nothing more than a reshuffle of the CV folds (area_worst, picked in our
single run above, rarely or never makes the cut here). A single lasso fit gives one
list; a stability check tells you which parts of it are real. Report the
stable core, not whatever one run happened to say.

### A connection worth knowing

The SVM is secretly a penalized method too. ISLR §9.5 shows the support vector
classifier solves

$$\min_{\beta}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \max\big[0,\, 1 - y_i f(x_i)\big] \;+\; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 ,$$

a **hinge loss** plus a **ridge** penalty — and $\lambda$ plays the role of
$1/C$ for the software cost. Swap the hinge loss for the logistic loss and you
have ridge logistic regression; swap the ridge penalty for the lasso penalty
and you have the lasso. "Regularization for classification" is one recipe —
**loss + penalty** — with interchangeable parts.

## Try it yourself

**1. Elastic net.** `alpha` between 0 and 1 mixes the lasso and ridge
penalties. Correlated features (radius, perimeter, and area are nearly the
same measurement) tend to enter *together* under the elastic net, where the
lasso picks one and drops the rest. Fill in an `alpha` and compare how many
features survive — and whether the test accuracy changes at all.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
#| exercise: ex_enet
set.seed(2155)
enet_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                     alpha = ______, nfolds = 10)   # try 0.5, then 0.1

b <- coef(enet_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
c(features_kept = sum(b[-1, 1] != 0),
  test_accuracy = mean(predict(enet_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se",
                               type = "class") == wtest$diagnosis))
```

**2. A different split.** In Part 1, change `set.seed(2155)` before
`createDataPartition()` to another number and re-run the part. Does the
linear kernel still hold its own against the radial one?

## Things worth remembering

- **Cost `C` in software is the opposite of the budget $C$ on the slides.**
  Tune it by cross-validation on a log-spaced grid, never by training error.
- **Try the linear kernel first.** On the tumor data a straight line is
  already as good as anything fancier; reach for a kernel only when CV says it
  helps.
- **With many correlated features, penalize.** Unpenalized logistic regression
  broke on 30 correlated features; the lasso kept the coefficients sane *and*
  selected a short list — but check how stable that list is before you
  interpret it.
